docs.title: Home
docs.text:
SHU SIT LAB · RESEARCH COMPUTING

Move from idea to GPU job.

A practical guide to using the lab's DGX Spark system: schedule GPU work with Slurm and run reproducible environments with Enroot and Pyxis.

Run your first job Try the LLM example

Compute DGX Spark Scheduling Slurm Environments Enroot + Pyxis

GPU workflow updated — 16 October 2026

Run GPU work in a Slurm allocation using an Enroot/Pyxis container. Ordinary SSH sessions on the manager cannot access the GPU. Read what changed for users, including shared homes, login-session limits and job history.

docs.title: Choose your next stepStart personal work in your home directory.
docs.text:
01 Get connected Set up NVIDIA Sync, check the system, and submit your first GPU job. Start here → 02 Follow a complete example Load a small LLM and run tests that verify its expected answers. Run the LLM test → 03 Run your own work Use a containerised environment for reproducible Python, CUDA, and ML workloads. Work with containers →

KEEP PROJECTS ORGANISED

Your personal $HOME is shared across all three nodes. Use it for project files, logs, and results; leave Enroot's working caches at their system defaults. Ask Josh about managed storage under /home/data and which nodes can access a project directory.

docs.title: What is on the system?
docs.text: Component What it is for DGX Spark NVIDIA GPU compute for research workloads Slurm Requests resources and runs interactive or batch jobs Enroot + Pyxis Runs containers directly through Slurm without sudo

docs.title: Need help?
docs.text: If a job fails or you need an account, contact Josh Bamforth at josh.bamforth@shu.ac.uk. The FAQ & Troubleshooting page covers common job and container issues.

docs.title: Cluster changes: what users need to do
docs.text: Updated 16 October 2026. These instructions apply to all ordinary cluster accounts, including accounts created later.

docs.title: Run GPU work through Slurm, inside a container
docs.text:
All GPU workloads must run in an Enroot/Pyxis container launched through Slurm. This includes training, inference, notebooks that use CUDA, and Ollama. Connect to the manager, spark-c3d8.local, to edit files and submit jobs. Request a GPU and start the container with srun; use sbatch for work that should continue after you disconnect.

On the manager, ordinary SSH sessions, personal background services and containers started directly from those sessions are blocked from GPU devices. A container by itself does not reserve a GPU. A CPU-only Slurm job also cannot use a GPU. The technical restriction enforces scheduled GPU access on the manager; using a container is the lab's required workflow for GPU jobs on every node.

Start with the first GPU job, interactive and batch examples, or container guide. Submit from the manager and let Slurm select an available node. Direct worker logins are not a way to bypass scheduling.

If you previously ran GPU work directly:

  1. Move the workload into a compatible container and request its CPU, RAM, GPU and time limit in Slurm.
  2. Stop your old background workload or personal service once its work is saved. tmux, screen, nohup, and personal services do not create allocations.
  3. Use the job ID, its log and sacct to check the result. Stop a server job when you have finished using it so its GPU becomes available to others.

docs.title: Keep login activity small
docs.text:
The manager's ordinary sessions and personal services have an existing aggregate limit of 8 GiB RAM and two CPUs' worth of CPU time per user. These are shared by all your ordinary processes on that machine, not separate limits for every terminal. Use the login shell for editing, submission and lightweight checks; schedule substantial computation, downloads/preparation that need more resources, and servers through Slurm.

Slurm jobs use the resources requested for the allocation. The login limit is not an 8 GiB GPU-memory allowance and does not reserve any GPU capacity.

docs.title: Your home follows you between nodes
docs.text:
Your personal /home/<username> is stored on the manager and mounted at the same path on both workers. Keep project scripts, inputs, logs and results there, and mount the project into your container. Matching usernames and numeric user and group IDs are managed across the cluster.

Only these personal homes are guaranteed shared by this setup. /shared is node-local despite its name. /home/data is managed storage on the manager; ask Josh about availability on other nodes before using it in a job.

Leave Enroot's runtime, cache and data paths at their system defaults. The workers have local per-user container storage. Redirecting those paths into your NFS home can create large shared-storage writes and stalls. Model caches and saved results are separate from Enroot's working files; arrange storage for large datasets and model collections with Josh. Keep another copy of important results.

Ask Josh to change or reset a password across the cluster. Running passwd on one machine does not automatically synchronize the other machines. Continue to use your own account and the SSH authentication method set up for it.

docs.title: Check your own queue and saved history
docs.text: Job history has been enabled since 12 October 2026. Ordinary users can see their own job details and history; administrators can see all users' records. An empty personal queue does not mean that the cluster is empty. Use sinfo for node availability, squeue -u "$USER" for your queue, and sacct after a job leaves the queue. See Job History for copyable commands.

docs.title: Choose resources for this cluster
docs.text:
There are three Sparks in partition gpu: spark-c3d8 (manager and compute node), spark-91d0 and spark-2c1b. Each has one GB10 GPU and 20 CPUs. Requesting two GPUs on one node cannot work here; multiple GPUs require multiple nodes and a distributed application.

The workers have a tested fast link to each other. The manager's fast-network connection is still awaiting cabling, and shared homes currently use its Wi-Fi connection. Ask Josh before scaling a communication-heavy workload across nodes. Adding --nodes=2 does not make a single-process training script distributed.

docs.title: Report storage or node problems
docs.text: If a job hangs while importing a container or writing files, collect the job ID, allocated node, last log lines and time, then contact Josh Bamforth. A drained node is intentionally unavailable. Administrators check it before returning it to scheduling; users should not try to clear its drain or reboot it.

docs.title: Containers with Enroot and Pyxis
docs.text:
Run every GPU workload inside a container launched through Slurm. Request the GPU and the container in the same srun command. Enroot is the rootless container runtime; Pyxis connects it to Slurm. You do not need sudo, Docker group membership or a Docker daemon on the Spark.

The manager blocks GPU access from ordinary login sessions and personal services. A container started directly from an SSH shell does not create a GPU allocation. See Cluster Changes for Users for the policy.

docs.title: Choose a compatible image
docs.text:
The Sparks use ARM64 (aarch64) CPUs and GB10 GPUs. An x86-only image or a framework that lacks GB10 support will not work. The examples pin NVIDIA's PyTorch 25.09-py3, which includes CUDA 13.0.1; see the NVIDIA release notes. Pin a version for reproducibility and check compatibility before changing it.

Pyxis accepts a registry image or an existing SquashFS file:

Image form Example NVIDIA registry nvcr.io#nvidia/pytorch:25.09-py3 Docker Hub ubuntu:24.04 (a CPU base image, not a complete GPU ML environment) Exported image file "$HOME/containers/my-project.sqsh"

Use the # separator for a non-default registry with the installed Enroot/Pyxis stack. The image file and its parent directories must be readable by your user on the allocated node. A file in your shared home has the same path on all nodes. The Pyxis usage guide describes its image and mount options.

docs.title: Interactive and batch commands
docs.text:
The Slurm guide contains complete interactive and batch GPU container examples. Both bind a project directory into /workspace, run as your ordinary identity, and request CPU, memory and time as well as a GPU.

Keep source, data and outputs in bind-mounted directories. Changes made only inside a temporary container filesystem may disappear when the job ends. Container preparation and model downloads count toward the job's time limit.

docs.title: Useful options
docs.text:
Option Purpose --container-image= Choose the image; required for the GPU workflow --container-mounts="host:container" Make project data visible inside the container --container-workdir=/workspace Set the application's working directory --no-container-remap-root Show your normal UID inside the container; this does not grant host privileges --container-writable Allow changes to the temporary container filesystem --container-name= Reuse a named container on the same node; it is not a cluster-wide image

Create mount source directories and log directories before submission. Keep credentials out of job scripts and logs.

docs.title: Application dependencies and custom images
docs.text:
Install project dependencies inside the job's container or build them into a versioned image. Avoid changing the host's Python/CUDA installation. A virtual environment alone is not a container and does not meet the GPU workflow.

For small Python additions, the LLM smoke test installs packages into a project directory inside its container. For a reusable environment, build an ARM64 image on a machine or CI runner with a suitable container builder, push it to an accessible registry, and use its pinned tag with Pyxis. Ordinary Spark accounts do not need host Docker access for this workflow. Ask Josh about private registry credentials and lab-provided images.

docs.title: Container working storage and model caches
docs.text:
Leave ENROOT_RUNTIME_PATH, ENROOT_CACHE_PATH and ENROOT_DATA_PATH at their system defaults. The workers have private per-user working storage on their own disks. /shared is node-local; its name does not mean that it is an NFS share. Do not redirect Enroot's working cache/data into your shared home or copy another user's expanded container directories.

Use your shared home for project files, exported .sqsh images and persistent application data. A Hugging Face or Ollama model cache is application data, separate from Enroot's working cache. Arrange storage with Josh for large model collections and datasets: shared-home traffic currently crosses the manager's Wi-Fi connection. /home/data is manager-local unless a project has separately been provisioned for other nodes.

docs.title: Ollama and other GPU servers
docs.text:
Run Ollama inside a GPU-allocated Slurm container, for the duration of a job. Use an ARM64/GB10-compatible image that contains Ollama. A host installation being present does not mean a personal login-session server is an approved GPU workflow. The recent GPU change did not remove host software.

If Josh has supplied a compatible image at the path below, this starts a server inside an allocation. Replace the image path with the actual supplied file:

mkdir -p "$HOME/ollama-models"
OLLAMA_IMAGE="$HOME/containers/ollama-gb10.sqsh"
if test -r "$OLLAMA_IMAGE"; then
  srun --account=hpc --partition=gpu --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 \
     --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=32G --time=02:00:00 --mpi=none \
     --container-image="$OLLAMA_IMAGE" --no-container-remap-root \
     --container-mounts="$HOME/ollama-models:/models" \
     env OLLAMA_MODELS=/models OLLAMA_HOST=127.0.0.1:11434 ollama serve
else
  echo "Set OLLAMA_IMAGE to a supplied compatible image" >&2
fi

This is a foreground interactive server; closing its allocation stops it. Ask Josh for connection/tunnelling instructions to the allocated node, which may be a worker. Check for a port conflict with another server before choosing a port. Use a batch job if the server must survive disconnecting, give it a suitable time limit, and cancel your job when finished.

Stop and disable an old personal Ollama service only if you previously created that service and have saved any work it is serving:

systemctl --user disable --now ollama.service

This command acts on your own service. It does not create a Slurm job or a replacement container server.

docs.title: Contributing to These Docs
docs.text: These docs are just Markdown files in the docs/ folder of this repo, built with MkDocs and the Material theme. Anyone in the lab can edit them.

docs.title: Quick edits (no local setup)
docs.text: Click the pencil/edit icon at the top of any page (or edit the file directly on GitHub), commit to a new branch, and open a pull request. GitHub will show you a live diff.

docs.title: Editing locally
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-ORG/YOUR-REPO.git
cd YOUR-REPO
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000 — it live-reloads as you edit files in docs/.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text: Just merge to main. A GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/deploy.yml) automatically rebuilds and redeploys the site to GitHub Pages on every push to main.

docs.title: Adding a new page
docs.text:
1. Create a new .md file under docs/
  2. Add it to the nav: section of mkdocs.yml
  3. Open a PR

docs.title: CUDA or nvidia-smi fails in my manager SSH shell
docs.text: GPU access is blocked for ordinary login sessions and personal services on the manager. Start a GPU-allocated container through Slurm using the interactive example. A virtual environment, tmux session or container started directly from the login shell does not allocate a GPU. Do not change device permissions or use sudo.

docs.title: My container cannot see the GPU
docs.text:
Check that the Slurm job requests --gres=gpu:1 and that the application is the command run by srun --container-image=.... A CPU-only allocation cannot use the GPU. Inside the allocated PyTorch container, check:

python -c "import torch; assert torch.cuda.is_available(); print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))"

Use an ARM64 image and a framework/CUDA version compatible with GB10. Errors such as exec format error or no kernel image is available can indicate an architecture mismatch. nvidia-smi inside the container is a useful driver check; an actual calculation also verifies that the application can use the GPU.

docs.title: My job is pending
docs.text:
Run squeue -u "$USER", then scontrol show job <job-id> and check Reason:

Reason Meaning Resources The requested resources are not currently available Priority Other eligible work has scheduling priority JobHeldUser You submitted or placed a hold; release it only when ready ReqNodeNotAvail A requested node may be down, drained or unavailable An association/QOS limit Check the exact reason with Josh; the shared hpc account itself adds no GPU quota

Use sinfo for node availability. Ordinary users see their own queue details; an empty queue does not show that the entire cluster is idle.

docs.title: I requested multiple GPUs and the job cannot start
docs.text: Each node has one GPU. --gres=gpu:2 requests two per node and cannot fit here. Multi-GPU work needs multiple nodes, one GPU per node, and an application with a correctly configured distributed launcher. See the resource guide.

docs.title: The first container or model download is slow
docs.text:
The first run may need to fetch and prepare a large image, then download model weights. Allow preparation time within the job limit and watch the logs. Check registry access/authentication if the log reports a pull failure. Do not launch many duplicate imports or redirect Enroot's cache/data paths into your NFS home.

For a persistent stall, report the job ID, node, timestamp and last log lines to Josh. A process waiting indefinitely for shared-storage I/O needs investigation; repeated cancellation or resubmission may not resolve the underlying problem.

docs.title: My home or project files are missing on a worker
docs.text:
Personal homes should be mounted from the manager at /home/<username> on each worker. Report missing or hanging mounts to Josh. Do not write replacement files into an unmounted home directory. A worker whose required homes fail to mount will not start its Slurm compute service.

/home/data and /shared are not automatically shared across nodes. Ask about the storage provisioned for your project, or place your project in your own shared home and bind it into the container.

docs.title: My manager shell or personal service runs out of memory
docs.text: Ordinary processes share an 8 GiB RAM / two-CPU limit per user on the manager. Submit substantial work through Slurm with suitable resources. These login limits do not describe the RAM allocated to your scheduled job or a GPU-memory allowance.

docs.title: My job disappeared from squeue
docs.text:
Check its saved history and application log:

sacct -j <job-id> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS,AllocTRES

History is available from 12 October 2026. Job-step rows often hold the memory measurements. See Job History.

docs.title: Where do job logs go?
docs.text: The paths in #SBATCH --output and --error determine this, usually under your project's logs/ directory. Create it before sbatch; Slurm needs to open the files before your script executes. A failed setup may have no application log, so check sacct and report the job ID if necessary.

docs.title: How do I change my password across the cluster?
docs.text: Ask Josh to make a synchronized change. A bare passwd command changes only the machine on which it runs. Keep using your own account and its configured SSH authentication; do not share another person's login.

docs.title: Who do I ask for help?
docs.text: Contact Josh Bamforth at josh.bamforth@shu.ac.uk. Include the job ID, allocated node, time and useful error text. Do not send passwords or private SSH keys.

docs.title: 1. Get an account
docs.text: Accounts are created individually — there's no self-signup. Email Josh Bamforth at josh.bamforth@shu.ac.uk to request access. You'll be given a username and asked to set a password, which you'll then use with the authentication method set up for your account. Use your own account. Josh manages account and password synchronization across the nodes; a password change on one node alone is not synchronized automatically.

docs.title: 2. Log in with NVIDIA Sync
docs.text:
Use NVIDIA Sync to connect to the manager with your own account. A normal SSH client also works once your account's authentication has been set up.

Download NVIDIA Sync from https://build.nvidia.com/spark/connect-to-your-spark/sync. Once installed, connect to the Robotics WiFi in Sheaf 4114. In NVIDIA Sync, add a device, give it a recognisable name, select Hostname or IP, and choose spark-c3d8.local. Enter your own account details from step 1. Submit jobs from this manager; Slurm starts them on the allocated node.

GPU work uses Slurm containers

Run training, inference and GPU servers inside a container launched with Slurm. GPU access from ordinary SSH sessions on the manager is blocked. Starting a container directly from your login shell does not create a GPU allocation. Read Cluster Changes for Users before migrating an existing workload.

docs.title: 3. Check the cluster is available
docs.text:
Once NVIDIA Sync has connected you and opened a shell:

sinfo

This lists node states. idle means free, alloc means fully in use, mix means partially in use, and down/drain means unavailable.

squeue

Ordinary users see their own jobs. Use squeue -u "$USER" to request your queue explicitly. Other users may be running work even when your queue is empty. Each of the three nodes has one GPU; sinfo shows overall node availability.

docs.title: 4. Your first GPU job
docs.text:
This example runs a short PyTorch GPU calculation in an NVIDIA container and writes its output to your shared home directory. Copy the commands into the shell opened by NVIDIA Sync.

mkdir -p "$HOME/first-training-job/logs"
cd "$HOME/first-training-job"

Create a file called first-training.sbatch containing:

first-training.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=first-training
#SBATCH --account=hpc
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail

srun --mpi=none \
     --container-image='nvcr.io#nvidia/pytorch:25.09-py3' \
     --no-container-remap-root \
     --container-mounts="$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:/workspace" \
     --container-workdir=/workspace \
     python -c "import torch; assert torch.cuda.is_available(); x = torch.rand(4096, 4096, device='cuda'); print('Training test completed on:', torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)); print('Result:', (x @ x).mean().item())"

Submit it and check its progress:

sbatch first-training.sbatch
squeue -u $USER

When the job is no longer listed in squeue, inspect its output. Replace <job-id> with the ID printed by sbatch.

cat logs/first-training-<job-id>.out
sacct -j <job-id> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode

If it reports Training test completed on, you have successfully run a GPU job. Keep your code and outputs in this project directory, then adapt the container command to run your own training script.

docs.title: 5. Storage
docs.text:
Use your own home directory ($HOME, /home/<username>) for code, working files, logs and results. It is stored on the manager and mounted at the same path on both workers. Bind your project into the container as in the example. Leave Enroot's container cache/runtime/data paths at their system defaults.

/home/data is managed storage on the manager. It is not automatically shared with the workers. Ask Josh which nodes can access a provisioned project path. Its main areas are:

Location Intended use /home/data/containers Lab-managed container assets /home/data/datasets Lab-managed datasets /home/data/scratch Temporary working storage for provisioned projects /home/data/shared Files shared through provisioned project directories

Do not create directories directly under /home/data. Ask Josh if you need a project directory there or access to a shared dataset. Do not rely on the Spark as the only copy of important results: copy finished work to University OneDrive or your own machine.

The directory /shared on a worker is local to that worker despite its name. Only your personal home is guaranteed shared by this setup.

Next, see:

  • LLM smoke test for a complete small-model example with answer checks
  • Submitting Slurm Jobs for batch scripts and job options
  • Containers (Enroot & Pyxis) for running your actual workloads in containers

docs.title: Job history and resource use
docs.text:
Slurm saves job history from 12 October 2026 onward. Your job leaving squeue means it is no longer queued or running; check its saved state to find out whether it succeeded, failed, timed out or was cancelled.

Run these commands on the manager, spark-c3d8.local, using your own account. Ordinary users see their own records. Administrators can view other users' jobs.

docs.title: Your jobs from the last seven days
docs.text:
sacct -X -S now-7days --format=JobID,JobName,Elapsed,State,ExitCode,NodeList

-X shows one summary row per job. A successful job normally reports COMPLETED with exit code 0:0. Read the output log as well: a job script must propagate application failures for its exit code to be meaningful. The examples in this wiki use set -euo pipefail for this reason.

docs.title: Details and memory use for one job
docs.text:
Replace 1234 with your job ID:

sacct -j 1234 --format=JobID,JobName,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,TotalCPU,MaxRSS,AllocTRES

Keep the step rows here: MaxRSS and CPU measurements are often recorded for a step such as 1234.0, rather than the top-level job. MaxRSS is the largest measured task resident-memory value, not the sum across all tasks. Sampling is periodic, so brief peaks may be missed.

AllocTRES describes the allocated CPUs, memory and GPUs. It does not measure continuous GPU utilization or GPU-memory consumption. A recorded GPU allocation alone does not prove that an application performed useful GPU work.

docs.title: Interpret the result
docs.text:
State Next step COMPLETED, exit 0:0 Read the log and check the application's outputs FAILED Read the error log and the job-step exit codes OUT_OF_MEMORY Check memory measurements and adjust the workload or RAM request TIMEOUT Check progress and request a suitable time limit for the next run CANCELLED The job was cancelled; the record may identify the cancelling user PENDING with JobHeldUser The job is held; it will not start until its owner releases it

To release a job you deliberately submitted with sbatch --hold:

scontrol release 1234

Only release it when its inputs and dependencies are ready. A held job is not doing computation and Slurm cannot predict when you will release it.

The shared accounting account is hpc; it is an administrative grouping, not a separate Linux login. Its existence does not add a per-user GPU quota. Jobs completed before history was enabled are not recovered.

docs.title: LLM smoke test: load a model and check its answers
docs.text:
This example downloads the small instruction-tuned model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, runs it on a GPU, and checks two deliberately simple answers. It is a useful first test of a new LLM workflow: if either answer is unexpected, the Slurm job fails and the job log explains why.

The model is about 0.5 billion parameters, so it is suitable for a quick single-GPU test rather than serious evaluation or training.

Run this from your account on spark-c3d8.local. The job requests a GPU and launches the model inside a container, as required by the current cluster workflow. Your shared home supplies the same project and model-cache paths on every allocated node.

Note

The compute node needs access to Hugging Face the first time this is run. The model is then retained in your personal cache under your home directory.

docs.title: 1. Create a project directory
docs.text:
Work in your home directory. Every account can write here.

mkdir -p "$HOME/llm-smoke-test/logs"
mkdir -p "$HOME/.cache/huggingface"
cd "$HOME/llm-smoke-test"

docs.title: 2. Add the Python dependencies
docs.text:
Create requirements.txt:

requirements.txt
transformers==4.48.3
safetensors==0.5.2

docs.title: 3. Add the answer checks
docs.text:
Create test_llm.py:

test_llm.py
import sys
import unittest

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer


MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct"


class LLMAnswerTests(unittest.TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        print("Loading tokenizer...", flush=True)
        cls.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)

        print("Tokenizer loaded. Loading model; the first run may download it...", flush=True)
        cls.model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
            MODEL_ID, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16
        ).to("cuda")
        cls.model.eval()
        print(f"Model ready on {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}.", flush=True)

    @classmethod
    def answer(cls, question):
        print(f"Asking: {question}", flush=True)
        messages = [
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": "Reply with only the requested answer. Do not explain.",
            },
            {"role": "user", "content": question},
        ]
        inputs = cls.tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
            messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt"
        ).to("cuda")

        with torch.inference_mode():
            output = cls.model.generate(
                inputs,
                do_sample=False,
                max_new_tokens=8,
                pad_token_id=cls.tokenizer.eos_token_id,
            )

        answer_tokens = output[0][inputs.shape[-1] :]
        answer = cls.tokenizer.decode(answer_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True).strip()
        print(f"Received: {answer}", flush=True)
        return answer

    def test_basic_arithmetic(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.answer("What is 2 + 2?"), "4")

    def test_capital_city(self):
        self.assertEqual(
            self.answer("What is the capital of France?"), "Paris"
        )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    runner = unittest.TextTestRunner(stream=sys.stdout, verbosity=2)
    unittest.main(testRunner=runner)

do_sample=False makes generation deterministic for a fixed model, prompt, and software stack. These are smoke tests, not a measure of an LLM's quality: for research evaluation, use a task-specific dataset and scoring method.

docs.title: 4. Submit the job
docs.text:
Create llm-smoke-test.sbatch:

The script has three parts: the #SBATCH lines request resources, the small background loop writes a status update every 30 seconds, and srun starts the container and runs the test. All messages go to one .out file, including normal Pyxis container-import messages.

llm-smoke-test.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
# Ask Slurm for the resources this small test needs.
#SBATCH --job-name=llm-smoke-test
#SBATCH --account=hpc
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out

set -euo pipefail

# Write a reassuring update while the first container or model download runs.
echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] Job started on $(hostname)."
while sleep 30; do
  echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] Still running - preparing the container, installing packages, downloading the model, or testing."
done &
heartbeat_pid=$!
trap 'kill "$heartbeat_pid" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT

# Run the commands below inside the GPU container. The first run may take
# several minutes while Pyxis imports the image. Pyxis cannot create directories so ensure all directories exist before running the job.
mkdir -p "$HOME/.cache/huggingface"

echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] Starting the container."
srun --mpi=none --container-image='nvcr.io#nvidia/pytorch:25.09-py3' \
     --no-container-remap-root \
     --container-mounts="$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:/workspace,$HOME/.cache/huggingface:/hf-cache" \
     --container-workdir=/workspace \
     bash -lc '
       set -euo pipefail
       echo "Installing Python dependencies."
       # Keep these pinned additions separate from the base packages.
       # The NGC image sets a pip constraint file for its base environment.
       PIP_CONSTRAINT= python -m pip install --disable-pip-version-check --target /workspace/.packages -r requirements.txt
       echo "Dependencies are ready. Loading and testing the model."
       PYTHONPATH=/workspace/.packages HF_HOME=/hf-cache python -u test_llm.py
     '

echo "[$(date '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')] All LLM smoke tests completed successfully."

Tip

bash -lc '...' in the srun command simply means “run these commands inside the container.” It first installs the two Python packages, then runs test_llm.py.

The job writes a timestamped progress update every 30 seconds, including while the container is being prepared or the model is downloading.

Submit it:

sbatch llm-smoke-test.sbatch

docs.title: 5. Watch the job and read the result
docs.text:
Check whether the job is waiting or running:

squeue -u $USER

Once sbatch prints a job ID, watch its output live. Replace <job-id> with that ID:

tail -f logs/llm-smoke-test-<job-id>.out

Press Ctrl+C to stop watching the log; this does not cancel the job. On success, the end of the log includes:

test_basic_arithmetic ... ok
test_capital_city ... ok

OK
[YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS] All LLM smoke tests completed successfully.

The first run takes longer because it downloads the container dependencies and the model. Later runs reuse the model cache and the Python packages stored in your home directory.

docs.title: Submitting Slurm jobs
docs.text: Submit from spark-c3d8.local, using your own account. Run GPU workloads in an Enroot/Pyxis container with a GPU allocation. The manager is also a compute node, so Slurm may legitimately place a job there. Ordinary manager SSH sessions cannot use its GPU. See the current user rules.

docs.title: Interactive GPU container
docs.text:
Create a project directory, then request a shell inside the container:

mkdir -p "$HOME/project"
cd "$HOME/project"
srun --account=hpc --partition=gpu --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 \
     --gres=gpu:1 --cpus-per-task=4 --mem=16G --time=00:30:00 \
     --mpi=none --container-image='nvcr.io#nvidia/pytorch:25.09-py3' \
     --no-container-remap-root \
     --container-mounts="$PWD:/workspace" --container-workdir=/workspace \
     --pty bash

Wait for Slurm to allocate resources and Pyxis to prepare the image. Inside the container, run your application or check GPU access with:

python -c "import torch; assert torch.cuda.is_available(); print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0))"

exit ends the shell and releases the allocation. An interactive job can end when its connection closes; use a batch job for unattended work.

docs.title: Batch GPU container
docs.text:
Put train.py in your project directory and create this file there:

train.sbatch
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=my-training-run
#SBATCH --account=hpc
#SBATCH --partition=gpu
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --gres=gpu:1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=4
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --time=04:00:00
#SBATCH --output=logs/%x-%j.out
#SBATCH --error=logs/%x-%j.err

set -euo pipefail
echo "Starting job $SLURM_JOB_ID on $(hostname) at $(date -Is)"

srun --mpi=none \
     --container-image='nvcr.io#nvidia/pytorch:25.09-py3' \
     --no-container-remap-root \
     --container-mounts="$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR:/workspace" \
     --container-workdir=/workspace \
     python -u train.py --epochs 10

echo "Training completed at $(date -Is)"

The image supplies PyTorch; add your application's other dependencies using the container guide. Create the log directory before submitting, because Slurm opens the logs before your script starts:

mkdir -p logs
sbatch train.sbatch
squeue -u "$USER"

The job continues after you close the submission terminal. Record its job ID. For an example with application code and dependencies included, follow the LLM smoke test.

docs.title: Watch progress and check completion
docs.text:
Container and model downloads can take several minutes on the first run:

tail -f logs/my-training-run-<job-id>.out

Press Ctrl+C to stop watching the log; this does not cancel the batch job. After it leaves your queue, check its log and saved result:

sacct -j <job-id> --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,MaxRSS,AllocTRES

See Job History for memory measurements, completion states and held jobs. sbatch accepting a job does not mean it has started or succeeded.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Command What it does sinfo Show overall node availability squeue -u "$USER" Show your queued and running jobs scancel <job-id> Cancel your job and release its resources sacct -X -S now-7days Show your saved job summaries scontrol show job <job-id> Show your job's resources, node and pending reason

Ordinary users see their own queue details and history. Administrators can see all users' jobs. An empty personal queue is not a cluster-wide utilization report.

docs.title: Request resources for this cluster
docs.text:
Each Spark has one GPU and 20 CPUs. The scheduler exposes 118000 MiB RAM per node. Request what your application needs, leaving time for preparation within the wall-clock limit.

Flag Meaning --account=hpc Use the cluster's shared accounting account --partition=gpu Use the partition containing all three Sparks --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 Run one task on one node --gres=gpu:1 Reserve the node's single GPU --cpus-per-task=4 Reserve four CPUs for the task --mem=16G Request job RAM on the node --time=04:00:00 Set the wall-clock limit --output= / --error= Choose logs whose parent directories already exist

A CPU-only job does not get GPU access. Increasing --mem does not allocate a GPU, and a GPU request does not replace a suitable RAM request. The manager's 8 GiB/two-CPU ordinary-login limit is separate from Slurm allocations.

For CPU-only work, omit the GPU request, for example:

srun --account=hpc --nodes=1 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --mem=4G --time=00:10:00 --mpi=none hostname

Use a container as well when the workload needs its own software environment.

docs.title: Multiple GPUs and distributed work
docs.text:
--gres=gpu:2 asks for two GPUs per node, which cannot fit on a Spark here. Two-GPU work needs two nodes, one GPU per node, and a program that launches distributed ranks correctly. Increasing the node count does not distribute a Python script.

The workers' MPI/NCCL communication has been tested over their fast link. The manager is awaiting fast-network cabling. Ask Josh for a suitable distributed container/launcher before scaling out. General examples use --mpi=none; the system-wide PMIx runtime is not available for srun --mpi=pmix.
